# The Usefulness of a Light

I have never been a keeper of anything more demanding than a houseplant, and yet I find lighthouses among the most moving structures human beings have built. I've been trying to work out why. Part of it is the setting: rock, weather, the horizon pulled tight as a wire. But I think the deeper reason is that a lighthouse is one of the few buildings whose entire purpose is to care for strangers. It doesn't shelter its builders, or make money, or glorify a god or a king, at least not primarily. It stands in a dangerous place and says, to people it will never meet: *here, not there.*

That is a strange thing for architecture to say, and stranger still that we've been saying it for over two thousand years.

## The Oldest Light

The most famous lighthouse ever built was on an island called Pharos, off the coast of Alexandria, and it was finished around 280 BC under the second Ptolemy. Accounts of its height vary, as ancient numbers tend to, but it was probably over a hundred meters tall, which would have made it among the tallest structures in the world for centuries. It was counted as one of the Seven Wonders. By day it was a smudge of pale stone, and by night, a fire burning at the top, perhaps with a polished reflector to throw the light farther, guided ships into a harbor whose approaches were low, flat, and treacherous. The Egyptian coast has almost no landmarks. A sailor coming from the open Mediterranean would see nothing at all, and then, if the gods were kind, a tower.

The Pharos was so successful as a word that in French, Italian, Spanish, and Romanian, the word for lighthouse still descends from its name: *phare*, *faro*. A building became a category. Earthquakes brought it down in stages over the centuries, and by the fourteenth century it was a ruin. Its stones were eventually used to build a fort on the same site. There is something fitting in that: the tower that was meant to keep people from wrecking on the coast ended as a rampart against them.

What interests me is that the Pharos was not built out of pure altruism. It was an advertisement. Ptolemy wanted ships to come to Alexandria, not to some rival port, and a spectacular beacon was both a service and a boast. This is the usual pattern with lighthouses. Their builders had mixed motives: trade, national pride, insurance rates, the fear of losing a cargo. But the effect of the mixture was benevolent. A ship doesn't care why the light is on. Self-interest and generosity are indistinguishable from the deck of a vessel at three in the morning.

## The Eddystone Problem

If you want to understand what it cost to make these things, look at the Eddystone Rocks, about fourteen miles off Plymouth in southwest England. They are a reef of gneiss that lurks just at the surface, in the path of ships making for the English Channel, and for centuries they killed sailors in large numbers. Building a light on them meant building a tower on a rock that the sea washes over in every serious storm.

The first attempt was by Henry Winstanley, an eccentric gentleman who had made his name in mechanical curiosities and trick entertainments. He built an elaborate, rather decorative wooden tower and lit it in 1698. It stood for five years. Winstanley was confident enough in his creation that he reportedly said he wished to be inside it during the greatest storm there ever was. The Great Storm of 1703 obliged him. In the morning, the tower was gone, and so was he. Only a few twisted iron bars remained in the rock.

The second tower, built by John Rudyerd, was cleverer, a tapered wooden structure ballasted with stone and built rather like a ship's hull. It lasted nearly fifty years and then burned, in 1755, when the lantern's candles set the upper structure alight. The oldest keeper, a man of great age, was said to have been looking upward when molten lead from the roof splashed into his open mouth. He survived the fire and, according to the story, died days later. Whether or not the details are exact, the incident tells you what the job was: keeping a flame alive at the top of a flammable tower on a rock in the ocean.

Then came John Smeaton, an engineer, and the third Eddystone light is the one I find most beautiful, because Smeaton solved the problem by thinking about a tree. He wanted a tower that would resist the sea not by being stubborn but by being shaped correctly, and he looked at the way an oak broadens at its base and narrows as it rises, swaying under wind while gripping the earth. He built a curved granite tower whose stones were dovetailed together like joinery, and he developed a hydraulic lime that would set underwater, which was a real advance in materials. It was lit in 1759 and stood for over a century. When the rock beneath it began to erode, the tower itself was still sound. It was taken apart and reassembled on Plymouth Hoe, where you can climb it today, a monument to the idea that you can defeat the sea by understanding it rather than defying it.

I think of this sequence, vanity, then cleverness, then patient observation, as a small history of engineering. Each failure taught something. And each was paid for, not abstractly, but in the lives of the people who stood in the towers.

## A Lens Made of Rings

For most of history the light itself was a problem. A fire on a tower needs fuel, and fuel means labor, smoke, and unreliability. Later towers used candles, then oil lamps with reflectors, but the light was feeble and much of it wasted, spilling in directions where no ship would ever be.

The breakthrough came in 1822 from Augustin-Jean Fresnel, a French physicist, who was interested in the wave nature of light and who solved a practical problem with theoretical elegance. A large lens capable of gathering and focusing a lamp's light would need to be immensely thick, heavy, and absorbent of the very light it was trying to send. Fresnel realized that the curvature of a lens is what matters, not its bulk. So he cut the lens into concentric rings, each a prism angled just so, and stacked them into a beehive of glass. The result was a lens that was thin, light, and astonishingly efficient. It could gather a small flame's light from every side and bend it into a single, powerful beam.

The first Fresnel lens went into service at the Cordouan lighthouse, on an islet in the mouth of the Gironde estuary, in 1823. Within a few decades it had spread around the world. There were "orders" of lens, from the enormous first order, taller than a person and glinting like a chandelier made of ice, down to small sixth-order lenses for harbors. Clockwork mechanisms rotated them so the beam swept the sea, and each lighthouse acquired its own signature: a flash every ten seconds, two flashes and a pause, a long white beam broken by a red one. A captain could identify a light the way you'd identify a voice. Lighthouses had *names*, in the sense that each one spoke in a distinct rhythm.

I love this. A lighthouse is not merely a lamp; it is a sentence. The coastline is a text of signals, and the sailor is a reader.

## The People Inside

The machines were only half of it. The other half was the keepers, and their lives were peculiar.

A keeper's job was mostly maintenance, and the maintenance was relentless. Wicks had to be trimmed, brass polished, lenses cleaned of soot and salt, clockwork wound at regular intervals, since the falling of a weight through the tower's core drove the rotation. Some larger lenses floated on a bath of mercury to spin with almost no friction, which was a marvel of engineering and probably not great for the health of the person breathing near it. Logs were kept. Weather was noted. The light had to be lit at sunset and extinguished at dawn, without exception, for years. A light that went out was not a minor lapse. It could be a grave.

The isolation varied. Some lights stood on the mainland with keepers' families in cottages beside them, and children grew up among prisms and paraffin. Others were rock stations, where men served rotations of weeks or months, cut off by weather, sometimes for longer than planned. Three keepers of the Flannan Isles light in the Outer Hebrides disappeared in December 1900, and no one has ever fully explained it. The most sober reading is that a huge wave swept them from a landing area, but the legend has grown: a table set for a meal, a chair overturned, an unfinished log. It endures because it touches something true about the work. These were people whose job was to stay alive, alone, in a place designed by nature to remove them.

And yet many keepers loved it. There is a long literature of contentment, of men and women who found in the routine a kind of clarity. You had a purpose that was simple and undeniable. Every evening, the light. The family of Robert Stevenson built lighthouses across Scotland for generations, including the Bell Rock light, which he completed in 1810 on a reef that vanished beneath the North Sea at high tide. His grandson, Robert Louis, was expected to join the family trade and instead became a writer, but he never quite lost the sense of the thing. He once said that his family's work was to "bring the light" to dark coasts, and that he'd have liked to be part of it. Writing *Treasure Island* was, perhaps, his own kind of lighthouse, though it warned no one of anything.

## Made Obsolete

Nearly all of this has ended. Electric lamps replaced flames, then automation replaced keepers, and satellites replaced sightlines. A modern ship knows its position to within a few meters from GPS, displayed on a screen on the bridge, and it does not need to squint into the dark for a flash. Lights have been automated across the world, and the human keepers are gone from almost all of them. In the United States, Boston Light, on Little Brewster Island, is the last with Coast Guard keepers, retained partly for reasons of heritage. Many old Fresnel lenses have been removed, some to museums, some to private collectors, some cracked and lost.

It is easy to mourn this. Certainly I do. But I have been trying to think about it a little differently, because the story of the lighthouse is not really a story of decline. It's a story of success. The lighthouse was a solution to a problem, and the problem has largely been solved. Fewer ships wreck now. The sea is no less indifferent than it was, but we have gotten better at navigating its indifference. To mourn the lighthouse too much is a bit like mourning the fact that smallpox is no longer around to be vaccinated against.

And yet obsolescence does something odd to a structure. Once a lighthouse is not necessary, it becomes visible in a new way. When a thing is useful, we see through it, to its function. When it's no longer useful, we see it. The tower becomes a tower, the lens becomes glass, the keeper's cottage becomes a place where someone once lived. What was practical becomes symbolic without anyone quite deciding that it should.

Many lighthouses are now maintained by volunteers, preservation societies, and local communities, who repaint the stripes, restore the stairs, and give tours. There's a poignancy in this: people caring for a thing that cared for others, returning a favor it never asked for.

## What a Light Means

I've come to think the lighthouse endures in our imagination because it embodies a moral idea that most of our institutions only gesture at. The idea is that there is a form of goodness that does not require knowing the person you help.

Most of our ethics is personal. We help the people near us, whom we can see and name. But a lighthouse helps people who are, by definition, absent. It helps the ship that is not yet in view, the sailor who has not yet made a mistake, the crew that will pass in the night and never know who kept the flame. Its generosity is addressed to the future and the anonymous. You can't thank a lighthouse. You can only, if things go well, not die.

There is something else. A lighthouse doesn't *rescue* anyone, exactly. It doesn't pull you from the water. It works before the emergency, at the level of information: this is where the danger is. It's preventive care rather than heroic intervention, which makes it less dramatic and more effective. Most of the good in the world is like this, unglamorous and easy to overlook. The bridge that doesn't collapse, the water that's clean, the train that runs on time: these are lights that stay on, and we notice them mainly when they don't.

I also find it moving that the lighthouse works by being *fixed*. Ships move; the sea moves; weather, tides, and fashions move. The lighthouse's whole value lies in the fact that it does not. It is the still point against which motion becomes legible. To navigate, you need something that stays put. This is true at sea, and I suspect it's true in a human life too. We orient ourselves by fixed things: a person who is reliably kind, a principle that doesn't bend under pressure, a home to which we can return. Being that fixed point for someone else is one of the great things one person can be. It's not glamorous. It mostly involves showing up, night after night, and doing the small thing that needs doing.

## The Light at Dusk

I'll end with an image, because the lighthouse is an image before it's an argument.

Imagine a stretch of coast at the end of a winter afternoon. The sky has gone the color of pewter, and the sea is a darker version of the same. The tower stands white against the gloom, and for a while it is only a tower, a piece of masonry, inert. Then, at the moment when the light has decayed enough that the difference matters, the beam begins to turn. At first it is barely visible, a faint brightening at the top. Then it sharpens. It sweeps out over the water in a long, slow arc, touches the edge of the darkness, and swings away. A few seconds later, it comes again.

Nothing about this is dramatic. No one is watching, perhaps. There may be no ship within twenty miles. But the light is doing what it has done for a very long time, from Pharos to the present, in towers of wood and stone and steel, tended by the vain, the clever, the patient, and the lonely. It says the same thing it has always said, in whatever rhythm belongs to that particular rock: *here, not there. Be careful. Someone was thinking of you.*

That last sentence is, I think, the whole of it. Someone was thinking of you. It's what we want from the world, and rarely get so plainly. The lighthouse says it in glass and fire, and does so for anyone who happens to be passing in the dark.

Whether or not we still need the light, I hope we never stop knowing how to build one.
